103	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.
104	
105	## The model program
106	
107	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.
108	
109	- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
110	- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.
111	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
112	
113	**count stage**
114	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.
115	
116	The code of this area is in these directories:
117	
118	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
119	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
120	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
121	
122	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
123	
124	## What the two paths share
125	
126	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
127	
128	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
129	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
130	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
131	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
132	
133	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
134	
135	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
136	
137	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
138	
139	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
140	
141	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
142	
143	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
144	
145	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
146	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
147	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
148	
149	It also refuses a function, method, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).
150	
151	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
152	
153	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
154	
155	## What the code generator does
156	
157	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
158	
159	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
160	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
161	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
162	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
163	
164	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
165	
166	## The run time
167	
168	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
169	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
170	
171	## Natives
172	
173	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
174	
175	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
176	
177	## Traps of the compiled path
178	
179	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
180	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
181	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
182	- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
183	  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
184	  - a call of a member that an api writes `abstract`, from a component that imports the api, where the component that exports the api leaves the member out or declares it at another header. The export check passes the exporting component. Declare such a member in it (`library.md`, "Designing a change"; ledger row 816).
185	
186	## The checker's gaps
187	
188	`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.
189	
190	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786). It accepts `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, whose declared domains are equal, and runs the generic one (ledger row 759).
191	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
192	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
193	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
194	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
195	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
196	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. The compiled path does not leave out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
197	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
198	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. A program that declares such a trait does not compile: the code generator refuses the trait's `where` clause (ledger row 701). Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes before it refuses the clause: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).
199	
200	## The `fortress` commands
201	
202	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
203	
204	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
205	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
206	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
207	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
208	
209	## Running
210	
211	    cd ProjectFortress
212	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
213	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
214	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
215	
216	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
217	
218	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
219	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.
220	
221	## Before an edit
222	
223	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
224	
225	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
226	
227	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
228	
229	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.
230	
231	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
232	
233	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
234	
235	## Testing an edit here
236	
237	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
238	
239	      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
240	      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
241	      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
242	      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
243	      bin/fortress run P
244	
245	  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
246	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
247	
248	## The checker's time
249	
250	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
251	
252	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 150 seconds, more under load. That is longer than the Bash tool's default time limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
253	
254	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
255	
256	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
257	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
258	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
259	
260	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
261	
262	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
263	
264	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
265	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
266	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
267	
268	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
269	
270	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
271	
272	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
273	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
274	
275	A node's hash starts from its class's name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks or a union's members, moves only where the change itself moves it. Such a move is a difference: keep the old order, or report the difference, as for any other.
276	
277	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
278	
279	The timing is a smoke test. It is there to catch a slowdown of several times, or of orders of magnitude: a change that makes the checker three times slower must show. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
280	
281	If you change the checker:
282	
283	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
284	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
285	
286	       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
287	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
288	
289	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
290	4. After the second pass, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite").
291	5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
292	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
293	
294	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
295	
296	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
297	
298	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
26	- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
27	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
28	
29	## Designing a change
30	
31	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
32	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
33	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
34	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
35	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
36	- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
37	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
38	- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. The parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count. In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`.
39	  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because they call `Float`'s natives, which answer `ZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:184-191`).
40	  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
41	  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.
42	
43	  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
44	- The compiled checker's export check matches an api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches a field by its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. It requires no component member for an api member written `abstract`. So declare each such member in the component too, at the api's header: a call of a missing one dies with `NoSuchMethodError` (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"). Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next.
45	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
46	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
47	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
48	
49	## Editing
50	
51	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
52	# Running tests
53	
54	**track**
55	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
56	
57	**shard**
58	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
59	
60	**code state**
61	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

63	## The two suites
64	
65	`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
66	
67	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
68	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
69	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
70	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
71	
72	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
73	
74	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
75	
76	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
77	
78	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
79	
80	The two suites work in the same way:
81	
82	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
83	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
84	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
85	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
86	
87	To run a suite:
88	
89	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
90	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
91	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
92	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

118	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.

120	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).

224	
225	Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.

227	1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. 232	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
233	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine

240	## The atomic runs
241	
242	The atomic runs compile fourteen programs, and run each one three times at four threads, in about a minute. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:
243	
244	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
245	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
246	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
247	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
248	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
249	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
250	        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
251	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
252	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
253	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
254	        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
255	      done
256	    done
257	
258	The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.

260	## The ladder regression
261	
262	The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:
263	
264	- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
265	- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.
266	
267	A file that moved gets a mark:
268	
269	- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
270	- MISSING: a file with no output.
271	- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
272	- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.
273	
274	DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
275	Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.
276	
277	To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:
278	
279	1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:
280	
281	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
282	       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
283	          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
284	       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
285	       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
286	           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
287	           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
288	           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh

291	2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
292	3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.
293	
294	If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.
295	
296	## Comparing with an earlier run
297	
298	- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
299	- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
300	- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.
301	# Committing and pushing
302	
303	**scratch**
304	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
305	
306	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
307	
308	## What to commit
309	
310	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
311	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
312	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
313	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
314	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
315	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
316	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
317	
318	## How to commit
319	
320	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
321	
322	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
323	
324	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
325	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
326	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
327	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
328	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
329	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
330	
331	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
332	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
333	
334	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
335	
336	## Pushing
337	
338	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
339	
340	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
341	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
342	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
343	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
344	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
345	
346	         git push origin main
347	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
348	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
349	
350	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
351	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
352	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

# Running and reviewing a batch

The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.

**batch record**
: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.

**base**
: Commit that the batch starts from.

**gather**
: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.

**merged-diff review**
: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.

**repair round**
: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.

**commit stage**
: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.

**reserved point**
: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.

**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. The gather needs `git status --porcelain` there to print nothing. Push nothing to `main` from any tree, or git refuses the landing's push.
- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

## The landing

The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. The gather clears each finding before its commit, through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or by a reworded entry. The merged-diff review clears any that is left in its corrections commit. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.

If the batch's push is held for the curator, take the steps below at once on the local commits. Only the push waits, and the parts of the routing that need the pushed hashes.

1. Sweep the batch agents' to-dos from the session's shared task list: `explorations/coordinator/tools/sweep-tasks.py --delete`. If another workflow still runs, add `--running`, which removes only the completed tasks. The agents write these to-dos themselves, and the harness shows the whole list to every agent.
2. Check that the commit stage folded the batch's entries into FACTS (`references/record.md`, "The pass").
3. Run the orientation workflow in update mode on the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries, since the revival part cites decisions in most rules. `git diff <base> -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md` lists them. The workflow writes new text for each section of `fortress-repo`'s `revival-changes.md` that they touch. Have the writer install the sections that its judge accepts (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).
4. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
5. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing").
6. File what the review finds in PLAN. Then make these moves yourself. The manual's section "After the landing: the coordinator's routing" gives `PLAN-history.md`'s heading for each landing and the form of the one line.
   - Move word for word into `PLAN-history.md` each item that the batch built, each question that the batch or the curator answered, and each stale item. A stale item is one that a decision or a landed change has made moot.
   - If another home holds an open item's whole text, cut it in PLAN to one line with a pointer there. If it holds part, first move the rest there. This holds for the review lists too: an entry that `review-queue.md` holds becomes such a line.
   - Repoint each citation of a moved item: `git grep -n 'PLAN\.md' -- explorations/coordinator/*.md explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md .claude/skills`.

154	## Gather
155	
156	The gather composes one local commit per approved rung on `main`; nothing is merged.
157	
158	- **The order.** First, a rung goes after every rung it lands only with (`landsOnlyWith`), so that no commit on `main` holds a rung without the rungs it needs: in climb batch 17 the old rule, which compared lines across files, put rung L's `2b1cd8e63` before rung W's `743eb5286`, and that commit alone fails `LibraryOverloadFamilies.fss:37` (`reviews/batch-17-review.md`, finding 2). Then the rungs that share a file go in the ascending order of their lowest edited line in that file, so that a later hunk does not shift lines a landed record cites; a line is compared only with a line of the same file, and rungs that share no file keep the manifest's order. Where two files order one pair both ways, the pair keeps the manifest's order. Any `file:line` a record cites that an earlier hunk shifted is re-anchored by symbol. Tests cite the specification by section, never by line, so no test is re-anchored.
159	- **Each rung.** Its net diff is applied with `git apply --3way --index`. A conflict in unrelated regions is resolved by hand; one in the same logic is returned, not guessed. Its files are written from the journal where the branch lacks them, by the commands the brief renders per rung. For a repaired rung, `REPORT.md` and `record.md` are always rewritten from the repair round's texts.
160	- **The record folded.** The FACTS entry under its area. A ledger note that adds a fact through `ledger.py note`. A change to what a row says (its claim narrowed, a half fixed, its test promoted or renamed, its notes at the limit) through `ledger.py rewrite N FILE`: the whole line, stating the gap as it stands now, not its repair history. A note refused for length goes in so, with the notes cut back; none is left out. New rows through `ledger.py add FILE --section TITLE`, each `NEW-<rung>-<n>` placeholder replaced with its number everywhere the rung's files and tests cite it, before the rung's commit. The handover line, in the batch's `RECORD.md`, "Handover lines" (the old handover file is retired into PLAN's first section, which the coordinator keeps). The rung's "Revival change" section is folded into no file: both its parts are copied, word for word, into the batch's `RECORD.md` (below), and nothing is written under `.claude/`. Through batch 13 the gather folded each entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md` as the rung wrote it, and the cold reader that followed made a question's handle findable instead of deleting it: that is how the coordinator's agenda reached the skill (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there").
161	- **Corrections still owed.** The skeptic's `leftForGather` items. 162	- **Text mismatches.** A text mismatch the decisions do not settle is filed, not blocking ("Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect", item 4).

166	A rung that did not land has its `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` taken out of its branch path by path, its findings folded under "Not landed", and its new rows added. None of its source is applied.
